summary:
Kaduna State stands under Nigeria's national framework, and its own criminal law adds two layers that a visitor has to read together. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity (June 2025) records that Kaduna separately adopted its own secular Penal Code in 2017, whose Section 259 punishes 'unnatural offences' (sodomy, lesbianism and bestiality) with up to 21 years' imprisonment and a fine, a ceiling above the federal 14-year maximum.

Running in parallel, the Kaduna Sharia Penal Code Law 2002 (Law No. 4 of 2002) applies to Muslims. Peter Ostien's annotated volume of northern Nigerian Sharia legislation records that the law was signed into law and came into operation on 21 June 2002, published in Kaduna State Gazette No. 17, Vol. 36, of 4 July 2002 at pages A15-A108 and bound with the Sharia Criminal Procedure Code.

The Home Office's twelve-state Sharia penalties table (section 8.4.3, ILGA-derived) gives Kaduna's maximum for liwat (sodomy) as death by stoning, and provides that same-sex acts between women are punishable at the discretion of the qadi, the Sharia court judge.

Ostien's annotation of the Kaduna text records that it is one of only three states whose enacted wording states 'Whoever commits the offence of sodomy shall be punished with stoning to death (rajm)', with no graduation between unmarried and married offenders, while the lesbianism offence is left to ta'azir, discretionary punishment.

Human Rights Watch (2004) reports that by 2002 twelve northern states had adopted some form of Sharia into their criminal legislation, and that those twelve states remain the only ones where Sharia courts hold jurisdiction to try criminal cases, Kaduna among them.
tangentialFactors:
Kaduna's 2017 secular Section 259 sets a 21-year ceiling for 'unnatural offences', which is seven years above the federal 14-year maximum for same-sex conduct, so the state-level statute is the harsher of the two secular provisions a visitor would face.

Human Rights Watch (2004) traces the twelve-state bloc to Zamfara's governor introducing the Sharia Establishment Law on 27 October 1999, in force 27 January 2000; by 2002 twelve northern states had followed, and Kaduna's own instrument was promulgated on 21 June 2002.

Within that bloc, Kaduna is distinguished by its enacted wording: one of only three states whose text mandates stoning to death (rajm) for sodomy without any unmarried/married graduation, while the corresponding offence against women is routed to judicial discretion rather than a fixed tariff.
localsOnly:
The Kaduna Sharia Penal Code Law 2002 applies to Muslims, so residents who are Muslim face both the Sharia layer and the secular 2017 Penal Code, while the secular Section 259 applies on its own terms to everyone else in the state.

For women, the Sharia offence of same-sex acts carries no fixed penalty in Kaduna's text: punishment is set at the discretion of the qadi, and the lesbianism offence is classified as ta'azir, discretionary punishment, which leaves the severity to the individual court.

Residents are exposed to a state-level secular sentence of up to 21 years plus a fine under Section 259, a higher statutory maximum than the federal provision carries.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Kaduna-specific enforcement incident, arrest, raid, prosecution or act of violence against a trans or gender-nonconforming person appears in this inventory; the record for the state consists of statutory text and penalty tables only, so current enforcement practice in Kaduna is unresolved.

The inventory contains no record of a rajm sentence being imposed or carried out in Kaduna, and no record of any case in which Section 259 has been applied; whether either provision has been used in court is not sourced here.

Nothing in the inventory addresses Kaduna-specific rules or practice on identity documents and gender markers, airport or border screening, bathroom and facility access, healthcare refusals, or hate-crime protection; those questions are not sourced for this state.

The Kaduna penalty row in the Home Office note is derived from ILGA material and published in June 2025; whether the table reflects any change after that date is unresolved.
